title: Low-Level Design — an interview field guide
subtitle: The canonical LLD/OOD interview problems asked across FAANG & big tech (2021–2026) — how to approach each, the class design, the design patterns that fit, concurrency concerns, extensibility, and the pitfalls that lose points. Every entry ends with a quiz. Built from a verified, adversarially fact-checked research pass.

tiers.name: Foundations
tiers.blurb: The principles and process every LLD interview is graded against — SOLID, the answer framework, patterns, and how you're actually scored. Read these first.

topics.name: What an LLD/OOD interview actually is
topics.premise: Low-Level Design (LLD) — also called Object-Oriented Design (OOD) or the 'machine-coding round' — is a distinct interview format, separate from the algorithms round and from high-level system design (HLD). You're given an open-ended prompt ('design a parking lot') and asked to produce a clean, modular, extensible set of classes — sometimes as running code. It tests design skill, not algorithmic trickery: there is no single correct answer.
topics.frequency: Very high — a standard round at Amazon, Uber, Atlassian, Microsoft, Flipkart, and the India hiring loops of most large US firms. FAANG generally (Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon) list OOD/LLD as an evaluated competency.
topics.why: Interviewers want signal on how you structure code that other engineers will maintain and extend. HLD asks 'how do the services and data stores fit together at scale'; LLD asks 'inside one service, how are the classes, responsibilities and interfaces arranged'. The algo round asks 'can you find an efficient algorithm'. LLD is the only round that directly probes maintainability and extensibility.
solutions: It's a skill, not a knowledge dump
HelloInterview: 'LLD is a skill, not a knowledge problem.' You can't memorise your way through — you must demonstrate the modelling process live.
Two common formats
(1) A 75–90 min machine-coding round where you write running code; (2) a 45–60 min whiteboard/discussion round focused on class diagrams and trade-offs.
Distinct from HLD
Don't draw load balancers and shards here. Stay at the class/interface/object level: responsibilities, relationships, and method signatures.
No single answer
The grade is on the quality of reasoning and the structure, not on hitting one 'right' design.

topics.takeaway: LLD is the maintainability round: turn an ambiguous prompt into clean, extensible classes — and narrate why.
topics.deepDive:
The Low-Level Design interview occupies the middle rung of the design ladder. Below it is the coding/algorithms round (data structures, complexity); above it is high-level system design (services, sharding, caching, capacity). LLD sits in between: you are inside one component or service, and the question is how the classes are arranged so the code is correct today and cheap to change tomorrow.

The format varies by company but clusters into two shapes. The 'machine-coding' round (common at Uber, Atlassian, Flipkart, and many India-based loops) gives you 75–90 minutes to write actually-running code — usually console-based, no UI, no database — that a reviewer then reads for structure, correctness on edge cases, and extensibility. The 'discussion' round (common in US onsite loops) is shorter, 45–60 minutes, and focuses on class diagrams, responsibilities, and trade-off conversation, with only illustrative code.

What unifies them is that there is no single right answer and the interviewer is reading your process. Two candidates can produce very different class hierarchies and both pass, because the grade is on clarity of responsibilities, sensible use of abstraction, handling of edge cases, and — the differentiator at senior level — whether the design absorbs a new requirement without a rewrite. This is why 'LLD is a skill, not a knowledge problem': you cannot recall the answer, you have to perform the modelling. The good news is that the modelling process is learnable and repeatable, which is what the rest of this guide teaches.

mcqs.q: What does an LLD/OOD interview primarily test?
options: Finding the most efficient algorithm for a problem
Turning an open-ended prompt into clean, modular, extensible classes
Sizing infrastructure and choosing databases at scale
mcqs.explanation: LLD tests design skill at the class/object level — modular, maintainable, extensible structures — not algorithmic efficiency (coding round) or infrastructure sizing (HLD).

mcqs.q: How does LLD differ from high-level system design (HLD)?
options: LLD covers load balancers and sharding; HLD covers classes
LLD is inside one service (classes, interfaces); HLD is across services and data stores
They are two names for the same interview
LLD is only about writing SQL queries
mcqs.explanation: LLD operates at the class/interface level inside a single component; HLD operates at the service/data-store level across the whole system.

mcqs.q: Which statement best captures the nature of an LLD interview?
options: There is one correct design you must reproduce
It's a knowledge test you can memorise
It's a skill — a live modelling process with no single right answer
It's identical to a LeetCode algorithms round
mcqs.explanation: 'LLD is a skill, not a knowledge problem' — the grade is on the modelling process and structure, and there is no single correct answer.

topics.name: SOLID & the principles you're graded on
topics.premise: Interviewers expect you to apply the five SOLID principles — Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion — plus the supporting maxims DRY, KISS, YAGNI, and the Law of Demeter. They also strongly favour composition over inheritance and programming to interfaces for loose coupling.
topics.frequency: Universal — SOLID is the single most consistently evaluated dimension across every LLD source.
topics.why: These principles are the vocabulary interviewers use to describe good and bad structure. A design that violates SRP (a 'God class') or OCP (must edit existing code for every new case) is the most common reason a candidate is dinged. Naming them as you make decisions gives the interviewer explicit signal.
solutions: S — Single Responsibility
Each class has one reason to change. A ParkingLot that also formats receipts and talks to the payment gateway violates SRP.
O — Open/Closed
Open for extension, closed for modification. Adding a new vehicle type or split strategy should not require editing existing classes — add a subclass/strategy instead.
L — Liskov Substitution
Subtypes must be usable anywhere their base type is, without surprises. If Square extends Rectangle but breaks setWidth, you've violated LSP.
I — Interface Segregation
Prefer many small, focused interfaces over one fat one. Don't force a class to implement methods it doesn't use.
D — Dependency Inversion
Depend on abstractions, not concretions. High-level modules take an interface (e.g. PaymentProcessor), not a concrete CreditCardProcessor.
Composition over inheritance
Favour has-a over is-a. It avoids brittle deep hierarchies and enables runtime flexibility (Strategy, Decorator).
DRY / KISS / YAGNI / Law of Demeter
Don't repeat yourself; keep it simple; don't build what you don't yet need; talk only to your immediate collaborators (avoid a.b().c().d() chains).

topics.takeaway: Name SOLID out loud as you design. The fastest way to fail is a God class (SRP) or a design that needs edits for every new case (OCP).
topics.deepDive:
SOLID is the shared language of the LLD interview, so it pays to internalise not just the acronyms but the failure they each prevent. Single Responsibility is about cohesion: when a class has one reason to change, a new requirement touches exactly one place. The classic anti-pattern is the 'God class' or a class named Manager/Helper/Processor that quietly accumulates unrelated duties. Open/Closed is the extensibility test the interviewer is really probing when they say 'now add a new vehicle type' — if your answer is 'I add a subclass or register a new strategy' you pass; if it's 'I add another branch to this switch statement and edit three methods' you fail. The two are linked: SRP keeps classes small so OCP is achievable.

Liskov Substitution is subtle and beloved by interviewers because it catches inheritance misuse. The canonical trap is Square-extends-Rectangle: it reads fine until code that sets width and height independently breaks on a Square. The lesson generalises — inheritance implies a genuine behavioural is-a, and when in doubt you should reach for composition. Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion together push you toward small interfaces and constructor-injected abstractions, which is exactly what makes code testable (you can pass a fake PaymentProcessor in a unit test).

The supporting maxims matter in the room too. YAGNI is a useful counterweight: interviewers do penalise over-engineering — twelve patterns bolted onto a tic-tac-toe game is as much a red flag as a God class. The skill is judgment: apply the principle that removes real, likely change, and stop. Say the principle name as you make the call ('I'll put the pricing behind a Strategy interface so it's open for extension') — this converts a silent good decision into explicit interviewer signal, which is what actually moves the score.

mcqs.q: An interviewer says 'now support a new vehicle type.' Your design lets you add a subclass without editing existing classes. Which principle does this satisfy?
mcqs.explanation: Open/Closed: open for extension (add a subclass/strategy), closed for modification (no edits to existing code).

mcqs.q: A ParkingLot class parks cars, formats receipts, AND calls the payment gateway. Which principle is violated?
mcqs.explanation: Single Responsibility — the class has multiple reasons to change (parking logic, formatting, payments). This 'God class' is the most common LLD ding.

mcqs.q: Which is generally preferred in LLD interviews for flexibility and to avoid brittle hierarchies?
mcqs.explanation: Composition over inheritance (has-a over is-a) avoids fragile deep hierarchies and enables runtime flexibility via patterns like Strategy and Decorator.

mcqs.q: Which supporting maxim warns against over-engineering a simple problem with unneeded abstractions?
mcqs.explanation: YAGNI — 'You Aren't Gonna Need It.' Bolting on patterns you don't need is penalised just like a God class.

topics.name: The 5-step answer framework
topics.premise: A repeatable process converged across multiple sources: (1) clarify requirements & use-cases, (2) identify core entities — the nouns, (3) design classes with relationships, interfaces and methods — the verbs, (4) implement clean code applying SOLID + patterns and handle concurrency, (5) verify with edge cases and exceptions. HelloInterview's suggested timing for a ~45-min round: requirements ~5 min, entities ~3 min, class design ~10–15 min, implementation ~10 min, verification ~2–5 min.
topics.frequency: This framework (or a close variant) is recommended by essentially every LLD prep source.
topics.why: The single biggest first-five-minutes mistake is jumping straight to code. Clarifying scope prevents you from designing the wrong thing, and narrating each step gives the interviewer the communication signal they grade.
solutions: 1. Clarify requirements (~5–10 min)

Ask about scope, scale, and the specific use-cases in and out of scope. 'Multiple parking floors? Multiple vehicle sizes? Do we handle payment? Is this concurrent?' Write the agreed functional requirements down.
2. Identify entities — the nouns
Extract candidate classes from the requirements: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, Payment. Nouns become classes/objects.
3. Design classes — the verbs

Define relationships (association, composition, inheritance), the interfaces, and the methods. Verbs become methods. Optionally sketch a UML class diagram — 'not mandatory, confirm with the interviewer.'
4. Implement
Write clean, testable code. Apply SOLID and the pattern that fits. Handle concurrency where the problem demands it (locks / thread-safe structures).
5. Verify
Walk through edge cases and exceptions: lot full, invalid ticket, concurrent access, null inputs.

topics.takeaway: Nouns → classes, verbs → methods. Spend the first 5 minutes on requirements, not code — and narrate every step.
topics.deepDive:
The framework is deliberately front-loaded: the cheapest place to fix a design is before any class exists. In the requirements phase your job is to shrink an intentionally-vague prompt into a concrete, bounded problem. Good clarifying questions probe three axes — functional scope ('do we handle payment, or just allocation?'), scale/constraints ('one lot or many; do we need concurrency?'), and explicit non-goals ('I'll assume no UI and no persistence unless you want them'). Writing the agreed requirements where the interviewer can see them turns ambiguity into a contract you'll be graded against.

The noun/verb heuristic is the engine of the middle phases. Underline the nouns in the requirements — parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, ticket — and those become your candidate classes. Underline the verbs — park, unpark, calculate fee, issue ticket — and those become methods, which then reveal which class should own each behaviour (the method's home is usually the noun it most naturally acts on). Relationships fall out next: a ParkingLot has-many ParkingFloors (composition), a Ticket references a Vehicle and a Spot (association), a Car is-a Vehicle (inheritance, if the subtype genuinely substitutes).

Only after the skeleton is agreed do you write code, and even then you implement the core happy path first, then layer patterns where a real variation exists (pricing strategy, spot-assignment strategy). Reserve the final minutes for verification — explicitly walking edge cases (lot full, lost ticket, double-park, concurrent entry) — because catching these out loud is exactly the 'Testing' dimension of the rubric. Throughout, the meta-skill is narration: every silent good decision you don't voice is signal the interviewer can't score.

topics.name: The design patterns that actually matter
topics.premise: A small core of patterns dominates LLD interviews. HelloInterview: four patterns — Strategy, Observer, State, and Factory — 'cover ~90% of LLD interviews', and patterns should EMERGE from your design decisions, not be forced in. Educative's top five add Decorator and Singleton. Broader toolkit: Command (undo/redo), Chain of Responsibility, Composite, Builder, Adapter, Facade, Flyweight.
topics.frequency: Pattern knowledge is evaluated in nearly every LLD round — but correct, motivated use is what scores, not name-dropping.
topics.why: Patterns are proven solutions to the exact variation points LLD problems hinge on: interchangeable algorithms (Strategy), state-dependent behaviour (State), one-to-many notifications (Observer), and object creation without hard-coded types (Factory). Recognising which fits is the senior signal.
solutions: Strategy
Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind an interface. Splitwise split types, parking fee calculation, spot-assignment policy. The #1 most useful LLD pattern.
Observer
One-to-many change notification. Notification systems, BookMyShow seat-availability updates, pub/sub within a process.
State
Behaviour changes with internal state, each state its own class. Vending machine (idle → has-money → dispensing), elevator, order lifecycle.
Factory / Abstract Factory
Create objects without hard-coding concrete classes. Vehicle creation, notification-channel creation. Pairs with OCP.
Decorator
Add responsibilities at runtime without subclass explosion. Coffee with add-ons, pricing modifiers.
Singleton
One shared instance. Use cautiously — global mutable state and thread-safety pitfalls; often a code smell if overused.
Command
Encapsulate an action as an object; enables undo/redo and queuing. Chess move history, text-editor operations.
Others
Chain of Responsibility (request pipelines), Composite (trees/file systems), Builder (complex construction), Adapter/Facade (integration), Flyweight (shared immutable state, e.g. chess pieces).

topics.takeaway: Master Strategy, Observer, State, Factory — they cover ~90%. Let the pattern emerge from a real variation point; never force one in.
topics.deepDive:
The reason a handful of patterns dominate is that LLD problems are built around a small set of recurring variation points, and each pattern is the textbook answer to one of them. When a problem has 'several ways to do X and we might add more' — how to split a bill, how to price parking, how to assign a spot — that's a Strategy: an interface with swappable implementations, which also happens to satisfy Open/Closed for free. When an object's behaviour depends on where it is in a lifecycle — a vending machine that behaves differently with no money, money inserted, or dispensing — that's State, with each state as its own class and transitions as explicit methods, replacing a brittle tangle of if/else on a status field. When one change must fan out to many interested parties — seats freeing up, an order status changing — that's Observer. And when you need to create objects but don't want callers hard-coding concrete types, that's Factory, which keeps the 'new ConcreteThing()' decisions in one place so adding a type is a one-file change.

The critical meta-point, stressed by HelloInterview, is that patterns should emerge from the design, not drive it. The failure mode interviewers watch for is a candidate who, having studied a pattern catalogue, bolts Singleton + Factory + Decorator + Observer onto a tic-tac-toe game to look sophisticated. That reads as poor judgment (and violates YAGNI). The senior move is the opposite: you get the responsibilities right first, notice a genuine variation point, name the pattern that fits ('these split rules vary, so I'll put them behind a SplitStrategy interface'), and move on. Singleton deserves special caution — it's the pattern most likely to be a smell, because it introduces global mutable state and thread-safety problems; interviewers often probe whether you reach for it reflexively. Knowing when NOT to use a pattern is as much of a signal as knowing the pattern.

mcqs.q: Which four patterns are cited as covering ~90% of LLD interviews?
mcqs.explanation: HelloInterview: Strategy, Observer, State, and Factory cover the vast majority of LLD interviews.

mcqs.q: A vending machine behaves differently when idle, when money is inserted, and while dispensing. Which pattern fits best?
mcqs.explanation: State — behaviour depends on the object's current state, each modelled as its own class with explicit transitions.

mcqs.q: Splitwise must support equal, exact, and percentage bill splits, with more possibly added later. Which pattern fits?
mcqs.explanation: Strategy — encapsulate each split rule behind a SplitStrategy interface; adding a new rule doesn't modify existing code (OCP).

mcqs.q: What is the recommended relationship between design patterns and your design?
options: Pick patterns first, then fit the problem to them
Force in as many patterns as possible to show breadth
Let patterns emerge from real variation points in the design
Avoid all patterns and write procedural code
mcqs.explanation: Patterns should emerge from design decisions, not drive them. Forcing patterns in signals poor judgment and violates YAGNI.

topics.name: How you're actually scored
topics.premise: FAANG/MANGA coding-and-design rubrics converge on four dimensions — Communication, Problem Solving, Technical Competency, and Testing — mapped to Strong Hire / Hire / No Hire / Strong No Hire bands. The final decision is holistic ('signals'), not a numeric cutoff, and criteria are roughly consistent across Google, Amazon, Apple, and Netflix even where terminology differs. LLD-specific lenses add: entities with clear responsibilities, class interaction, extensibility, and communication of trade-offs.
topics.frequency: The 4-dimension rubric is the verified industry standard (techinterviewhandbook.org).
topics.why: Knowing the rubric lets you allocate effort to what's scored: talking (Communication) and edge cases (Testing) are graded dimensions that candidates routinely under-invest in, over-focusing on Technical Competency alone.
solutions: Communication
Clarifying questions, narrating trade-offs, thinking out loud. An under-rated, explicitly-scored dimension.
Problem Solving
Decomposition, handling ambiguity, structured approach.
Technical Competency
Clean code, correct abstractions, DRY, appropriate patterns, sound class structure.
Testing
Edge cases, exceptions, verifying the design works — call these out explicitly.
LLD-specific extras
Clear responsibilities per entity, sensible class interaction, and extensibility ('can it change without a rewrite?').
Bands
Strong Hire / Hire / No Hire / Strong No Hire (some loops add a middle band). Mixed results trigger interviewer discussion of signals.

How to prepare for LLD — HelloInterview
topics.takeaway: Four dimensions: Communication, Problem Solving, Technical Competency, Testing. Beware fake 'weighted %' rubrics online — the percentages are invented.
topics.deepDive:
The most useful thing to internalise about scoring is that Technical Competency is only one of four dimensions, yet it's where anxious candidates spend nearly all their energy. The Tech Interview Handbook's rubric — the best-corroborated public description of how FAANG loops grade — weights Communication, Problem Solving, and Testing alongside it, and these are precisely the areas strong coders neglect. A candidate who silently produces an elegant class hierarchy but never voices a trade-off, never asks a clarifying question, and never mentions an edge case can genuinely score worse than a candidate with a slightly messier design who narrates decisions, weighs alternatives, and enumerates failure cases. The rubric rewards the second candidate on three of four axes.

The scoring is holistic rather than arithmetic. Interviewers assign a per-dimension read and roll it up to a band — Strong Hire, Hire, No Hire, Strong No Hire — and in the debrief they argue from 'signals' (concrete moments: 'she caught the concurrent-entry race unprompted'; 'he needed heavy hints to decompose the problem'). This is why specific, voiced moments matter more than a polished silent artifact: signals are what get quoted in the room. It also means a mixed performance isn't averaged into a pass — a serious red flag on one dimension (say, a God class defended when challenged) can sink an otherwise good interview.

A practical warning the research surfaced: do not trust the neat 'weighted percentage' rubrics that circulate on prep blogs (e.g. 'Code Design 30%, Functionality 25%…'). That specific breakdown was traced to a single commercial site, has no company attribution, and was refuted under verification. Real companies publish dimensions, not percentages, and the final call is a judgment, not a weighted sum. Prepare to the four real dimensions, and treat any site quoting exact weights as marketing rather than fact.

topics.name: Design a Parking Lot
topics.premise: The single most-asked LLD problem and the canonical warm-up. Model a multi-floor parking lot with different spot sizes (motorcycle/compact/large), vehicle types, ticketing on entry, spot assignment, and fee calculation on exit. Frequently extended with payment, multiple entry/exit gates, and concurrency.
topics.frequency: Ranked #1 across essentially every source; the 'classic starter'. Commonly reported at Amazon and in machine-coding loops.
topics.why: It's rich enough to exercise inheritance (vehicle/spot hierarchies), Strategy (fee calculation, spot assignment), Factory (vehicle/spot creation), and concurrency (two cars racing for the last spot) — yet small enough to finish in an hour.
solutions: Core entities
ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot (with size), Vehicle (Motorcycle/Car/Truck), Ticket, EntryGate/ExitGate, Payment.
Spot & vehicle hierarchy
Abstract Vehicle with subtypes; ParkingSpot with a size enum or subtypes. Use LSP-safe hierarchies; prefer an enum + capability check over deep inheritance if simpler.
Strategy — spot assignment
SpotAssignmentStrategy (nearest, by-size-fit) behind an interface, so policy changes don't edit the lot.
Strategy — pricing
FeeStrategy / PricingStrategy (hourly, flat, day-rate) behind an interface — Open/Closed for new rate plans.
Factory
VehicleFactory / SpotFactory to create the right subtype without hard-coding.
Concurrency
Two vehicles must not be assigned the same last spot. Guard spot allocation with a lock or an atomic/thread-safe structure; make assignment a single synchronized critical section.
topics.papers: Sources: designgurus.io Grokking OOD; educative.io Grokking LLD; github.com/ashishps1/awesome-low-level-design; prakalpana.com. Verified.
topics.takeaway: Vehicle/spot hierarchy + Strategy for pricing & assignment + Factory for creation + a lock on the last-spot race. Nail this one first.
topics.deepDive:
The parking lot endures as the canonical opener because it maps the whole LLD toolkit onto a domain everyone already understands, so the interviewer can focus entirely on how you model rather than on explaining the problem. Start by clarifying scope, because the 'right' design depends on the answers: how many floors, how many spot sizes, do motorcycles fit in car spots (usually yes, not vice-versa), do we handle payment, multiple gates, and — crucially — is it concurrent? Each yes adds a class or a strategy; pinning them down first prevents rework.

The entity skeleton is a ParkingLot composed of ParkingFloors, each composed of ParkingSpots; a Vehicle hierarchy; a Ticket that binds a Vehicle to a Spot and an entry time; and gates. Two variation points immediately call for Strategy. Spot assignment ('nearest to entrance', 'best-fit by size', 'balanced across floors') is a policy that should live behind a SpotAssignmentStrategy interface so the lot doesn't hard-code it. Pricing ('flat', 'hourly', 'progressive', 'weekend rate') is the second, behind a FeeStrategy — this is the part interviewers most often mutate ('now add a night rate') to test Open/Closed, and a Strategy makes that a new class rather than an edit. A Factory for vehicles/spots keeps construction decisions in one place.

The part that separates a Hire from a Strong Hire is concurrency. In a real lot with multiple entry gates, two cars can request the last compact spot simultaneously; a naive 'find free spot, then mark it taken' has a check-then-act race that double-assigns. The fix is to make allocation a single atomic critical section — a lock around the find-and-reserve, or a thread-safe/atomic reservation on the spot — and to talk through it explicitly. Finish with edge cases: lot full (reject gracefully), lost ticket (penalty flow), a vehicle that fits no spot size, and idempotent exit. Voicing the race and the edge cases is exactly the Testing and Communication signal the rubric rewards.

options: Two vehicles being assigned the same last spot via a check-then-act race
The database running out of connections

topics.name: Design a Vending Machine
topics.premise: Model a vending machine that accepts coins/notes, selects a product, dispenses it with change, and handles sold-out and insufficient-funds cases. The textbook vehicle for the State pattern: the machine behaves differently in Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing, and SoldOut states.
topics.frequency: Tier-1 classic; appears in nearly every LLD list and has been reported tagged to Amazon onsite.
topics.why: It's the cleanest demonstration of the State pattern — replacing sprawling if/else on a status field with a set of state classes and explicit transitions — while also touching inventory, payment, and change-making.
solutions: State pattern
VendingMachineState interface with IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispensingState, SoldOutState. Each state implements the same operations differently and returns the next state.
Core entities
VendingMachine (context, holds current state), Inventory/ItemShelf, Product, Coin/Note denominations, ChangeDispenser.
Transitions
insertMoney(), selectProduct(), dispense(), refund(). Illegal actions in a state are rejected by that state's implementation.
Change-making
Compute change from available denominations; handle 'exact change only' when the machine can't make change.
Concurrency
If shared, guard inventory decrement and money handling so two buyers can't over-draw the same last item.
topics.takeaway: State pattern is the whole point: Idle → HasMoney → Dispensing → back to Idle, each a class. Don't model it with an if/else on a status enum.
topics.deepDive:
The vending machine is the interview's purpose-built showcase for the State pattern, and the fastest way to signal seniority is to reach for it deliberately instead of the naive approach. The naive approach models state as an enum field and scatters if (state == HASMONEY) checks through every method; it works for the demo but rots the moment a new state or transition appears, and it's exactly the brittleness interviewers are testing for. The State pattern instead makes each state a class implementing a common VendingMachineState interface, with the machine (the 'context') holding a reference to the current state and delegating every operation to it. Idle accepts money and moves to HasMoney; HasMoney accepts a selection and moves to Dispensing; Dispensing vends, returns change, and moves back to Idle or SoldOut. Illegal actions — pressing dispense while Idle — are simply rejected inside the state that owns that rule, so the invalid-transition logic is localised rather than smeared across the machine.

Around the state machine sit the supporting concerns. Inventory (an ItemShelf per product slot with counts) governs SoldOut transitions. Payment and change-making are their own responsibility: given the inserted amount and the price, compute change from available denominations, and handle the genuinely tricky 'can't make exact change' case by refusing the sale or requiring exact money — a good edge case to raise unprompted. If the machine is shared/concurrent, the inventory decrement and the money/change handling must be atomic so two simultaneous buyers can't both claim the last can or both receive change that empties the coin hopper. Rounding out with edge cases — refund mid-transaction, power loss during dispense (idempotency), invalid denominations — hits the Testing dimension. The headline, though, is always the State pattern: naming it and drawing the four state classes with their transitions is the move that earns the score.

mcqs.explanation: State — the machine behaves differently in Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing, and SoldOut, each modelled as a state class with explicit transitions.

options: A single large if/else switch on a status enum scattered through every method

topics.name: Design an Elevator System
topics.premise: Model one or more elevators serving a building: request handling (external hall calls + internal car calls), a scheduling/dispatch algorithm, direction and door state, and multi-car coordination. Combines the State pattern (moving up/down/idle, doors open/closed) with a pluggable scheduling Strategy.
topics.frequency: Tier-1; appears on every major list (HelloInterview, AlgoMaster, Prakalpana) and is a common machine-coding problem.
topics.why: It forces you to separate mechanism (car movement, doors) from policy (which car serves which request, in what order) — a clean Strategy boundary — and to reason about concurrency (many requests arriving asynchronously).
solutions: Core entities
ElevatorSystem/Controller, Elevator (car), Request (source floor, direction / destination), Door, Display, plus Button types (HallButton, CarButton).
State
Elevator direction/motion state (MovingUp, MovingDown, Idle) and door state (Open, Closed) as states or enums with guarded transitions.
Strategy — dispatch
SchedulingStrategy / DispatchStrategy interface (e.g. nearest-car, SCAN/LOOK elevator algorithm, destination-dispatch) so the selection policy is swappable.
Request handling
A queue of pending requests per car; the strategy decides ordering (often serve all requests in the current direction first, then reverse — the LOOK algorithm).
Concurrency
Requests arrive from many floors concurrently; the controller must enqueue/assign thread-safely, and each car processes its queue without losing requests.
links: How to prepare for LLD — HelloInterview
topics.takeaway: Split mechanism (State: motion + doors) from policy (Strategy: dispatch/scheduling). Keep the request queue thread-safe.
topics.deepDive:
The elevator problem's whole lesson is the separation of mechanism from policy, and interviewers grade on whether you draw that line cleanly. Mechanism is the physical behaviour: a car moves up, down, or sits idle; doors open and close; a display updates. This is naturally a small state machine, with guarded transitions (you can't open doors mid-travel, can't reverse without stopping). Policy is the decision of which elevator answers a call and in what order it serves its pending stops — and this is the part that genuinely varies (nearest-car, the SCAN/LOOK 'sweep' algorithm, or modern destination-dispatch that groups riders by target floor). Putting policy behind a SchedulingStrategy interface means you can demonstrate one algorithm and gesture at swapping it, which is the Open/Closed and Strategy signal in one move.

Modelling requests carefully matters. There are two kinds: external hall calls (a person on floor 7 pressing 'down', which only specifies a direction) and internal car calls (a rider inside pressing '3', a concrete destination). The dispatcher assigns hall calls to a car; each car maintains its own ordered set of stops. The classic LOOK behaviour — keep serving stops in the current direction until none remain, then reverse — is worth stating explicitly because it prevents the naive FIFO queue that makes the car yo-yo inefficiently. This is also where you show judgment about scope: a single-car version is fine to build first, then extend to N cars with the dispatcher choosing among them.

Concurrency is intrinsic here rather than bolted on: hall buttons on many floors are pressed asynchronously, so the controller's request intake and per-car queues must be thread-safe, and no request may be dropped or double-served under contention. A good candidate enqueues requests through a synchronized/concurrent structure and has each car consume its queue independently. Rounding out with edge cases — request for the current floor, all cars busy, a car taken out of service, overload sensor — covers Testing. The recurring theme to voice: mechanism is a state machine, policy is a strategy, and the two must not bleed into each other.

options: Specify only a direction, not a destination floor
mcqs.explanation: A hall call ('down' on floor 7) specifies only direction; a car call ('3') specifies a concrete destination. The dispatcher assigns hall calls to a car.

topics.name: Design an ATM
topics.premise: Model an ATM: card authentication (PIN), transaction selection (withdraw, deposit, balance, mini-statement), cash dispensing with denomination breakdown, and interaction with a bank backend. A strong State-pattern problem (Idle → CardInserted → Authenticated → TransactionSelected → Dispensing) with clear responsibility separation.
topics.frequency: Tier-2 classic; on the DesignGurus 16-problem OOD canon and most LLD lists.
topics.why: It exercises the State pattern for the session lifecycle, Strategy/Chain for cash-dispensing denominations, and forces clean separation between the ATM hardware, the session, and the bank service.
solutions: State pattern
ATMState: IdleState, HasCardState, AuthenticatedState, SelectOperationState, DispensingState. Each guards which actions are legal.
Core entities
ATM, Card, Account, BankService (backend), CashDispenser, Screen/Keypad, Transaction (Withdraw/Deposit/BalanceInquiry).
Cash dispensing — Chain of Responsibility
Dispense the requested amount as notes: a chain of denomination handlers (₹2000 → ₹500 → ₹100) each dispensing what it can and passing the remainder on.
Transaction hierarchy
Abstract Transaction with subtypes; keeps operations Open/Closed for new transaction types.
Edge cases & security
Wrong PIN (limited retries → card block), insufficient funds, insufficient ATM cash, amount not composable from available denominations, session timeout.
topics.papers: Sources: designgurus.io Grokking OOD (16-problem canon); educative.io Grokking LLD; awesome-low-level-design. Verified.
topics.takeaway: Session lifecycle = State pattern; note breakdown = Chain of Responsibility; keep ATM, session, and BankService as separate responsibilities.
topics.deepDive:
The ATM is really two design lessons wearing one prompt: a session state machine and a cash-dispensing algorithm, wrapped in a clean-separation-of-concerns test. The session is a natural State pattern — the machine is Idle until a card is inserted, then HasCard until a PIN authenticates, then Authenticated where an operation is chosen, then in a transaction-specific state, then Dispensing, then back to Idle when the card is ejected. Modelling each phase as a state class localises the rules about what's legal when (you can't withdraw before authenticating, can't authenticate without a card) and makes session timeout and card-eject uniform transitions rather than special cases sprinkled everywhere.

Cash dispensing is the second showcase, and Chain of Responsibility is the elegant fit. To dispense, say, ₹3,600 you want the largest notes first: a ₹2000 handler dispenses one and passes ₹1,600 down; a ₹500 handler dispenses three and passes ₹100; a ₹100 handler dispenses one and the remainder is zero. Each handler knows only its denomination and the 'next' handler, so adding or removing a denomination is a chain edit, not a rewrite. This also surfaces a great edge case to raise: an amount that can't be composed from available notes (or from the notes currently loaded), which the machine must reject before touching the account.

The separation-of-concerns axis is where responsibility discipline is graded. The ATM (hardware/session orchestration), the CashDispenser (physical cash logic), and the BankService (authentication, balance, debit/credit against the real account) are distinct responsibilities that must not be merged into one class. In particular, the money-movement should be transactional on the bank side and only reflected after a successful dispense, so a jam mid-dispense doesn't debit a customer who got no cash — an idempotency/consistency point worth voicing. Finish with the security edge cases: limited PIN retries then card block, insufficient funds, insufficient machine cash, and session timeout. Naming State for the session and Chain of Responsibility for the notes, while keeping the three services separate, is the combination that scores.

mcqs.q: Which pattern best models the ATM session lifecycle (Idle → HasCard → Authenticated → Dispensing)?
mcqs.explanation: State — each session phase is a class that guards which actions are legal, making timeouts and card-eject uniform transitions.

mcqs.q: Which pattern elegantly breaks a withdrawal amount into note denominations?
mcqs.explanation: Chain of Responsibility — each denomination handler dispenses what it can and passes the remainder to the next handler.

mcqs.q: Why should cash only be debited after a successful dispense?
options: So a jam mid-dispense doesn't debit a customer who received no cash (consistency/idempotency)
mcqs.explanation: Money movement must be consistent with physical dispensing — debiting before a failed dispense would take money without giving cash.

tiers.name: Games & boards
tiers.blurb: Board and game problems test rich domain modelling, move validation, turn/state management, and undo/redo. Interviewers love them because the rules create natural class boundaries.

topics.name: Design a Chess Game
topics.premise: Model a chess game: an 8×8 board, six piece types each with distinct movement rules, turn management, move validation (including check/checkmate/castling/en passant), and often move history with undo/redo. A showcase for polymorphism (per-piece move rules), Strategy, and the Command pattern (reversible moves).
topics.frequency: Tier-1 classic; on virtually every list (DesignGurus, Prakalpana, awesome-low-level-design).
topics.why: The six pieces are a natural polymorphism/Strategy exercise (each validates its own moves), the move log is the textbook Command-pattern use (undo/redo), and check/checkmate detection tests careful state reasoning.
solutions: Piece polymorphism / Strategy
Abstract Piece with subclasses (King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, Pawn) each implementing canMove(from, to, board) / getValidMoves(). Or a MovementStrategy per piece.
Core entities
Board, Cell/Square, Piece hierarchy, Player, Move, Game (orchestrator), MoveValidator, plus a GameState (active, check, checkmate, stalemate).
Command pattern — moves
Each Move is a command with execute()/undo(), enabling move history, undo/redo, and replay.
Rules engine
Validate legality (piece rule + not leaving own king in check), special moves (castling, en passant, promotion), and detect check/checkmate/stalemate.
Flyweight (optional)
Immutable piece-type data can be shared via Flyweight if modelling many games.
topics.papers: Sources: designgurus.io Grokking OOD; github.com/ashishps1/awesome-low-level-design; prakalpana.com. Verified.
topics.takeaway: Each piece owns its move rules (polymorphism/Strategy); model moves as Command objects for undo/redo; a separate validator handles check/checkmate.
topics.deepDive:
Chess is prized because its rules carve out class boundaries almost automatically, and the interviewer watches whether you let them. The centrepiece is piece polymorphism: an abstract Piece with a canMove or getValidMoves method, overridden per type, so the board never contains a giant switch on piece type — a rook slides orthogonally, a knight jumps in its L, a bishop diagonally, and each encodes that itself. This is Open/Closed in action: a chess variant with a new piece is a new subclass, not an edit to a monster method. Some candidates phrase this as a MovementStrategy per piece; either framing scores as long as movement logic lives with the piece, not in the board or the game loop.

The second showcase is the Command pattern for moves. Modelling each Move as an object with execute() and undo() — capturing what moved, from where, what was captured — turns move history, undo/redo, and game replay into first-class features rather than afterthoughts. This is the feature interviewers most often ask you to add ('now support takeback'), and a Command-based design absorbs it trivially while a mutate-the-board-in-place design does not. It pairs naturally with a Board that can apply and revert commands.

The subtle part, and where seniority shows, is the rules engine and its separation from movement. A move being geometrically legal for the piece is necessary but not sufficient: it's illegal if it leaves your own king in check, and the game must detect check, checkmate, and stalemate. Keeping this in a MoveValidator / rules component separate from the pieces avoids entangling 'how a bishop moves' with 'is the king safe'. Special moves — castling (two pieces, conditions on prior movement and intervening check), en passant (state from the previous move), promotion — are excellent edge cases to enumerate, and they justify the move-history state. Turn management and a GameState enum (active/check/checkmate/stalemate/draw) round it out. The winning narration: pieces own movement (polymorphism), moves are Commands (undo/redo), and a separate validator owns king-safety and end-game detection.

mcqs.q: How should per-piece movement rules be modelled?
options: A giant switch on piece type in the Board class
Each piece subclass overrides its own canMove/getValidMoves (polymorphism)
A single global function with if/else per piece
Store all moves in the database
mcqs.explanation: Polymorphism: each Piece subclass owns its movement rule, keeping the board free of a type switch and making new pieces Open/Closed.

mcqs.q: Which pattern makes chess move history, undo, and redo natural?
mcqs.explanation: Command — each Move is an object with execute()/undo(), so history/undo/redo/replay come for free.

mcqs.q: Why keep check/checkmate detection in a separate validator rather than inside the pieces?
options: To avoid entangling 'how a piece moves' with 'is the king safe' — different responsibilities
mcqs.explanation: Geometric legality (piece movement) and king-safety/end-game detection are distinct responsibilities; separating them keeps each cohesive (SRP).

topics.name: Design Tic-Tac-Toe
topics.premise: Model an n×n tic-tac-toe (or generalised board game): players, a board, placing marks, turn alternation, and win/draw detection. Often the warm-up before chess; also a place where interviewers test whether you AVOID over-engineering.
topics.frequency: Tier-1 classic and a common first game problem; appears on most lists.
topics.why: Small enough that the trap is over-engineering (bolting on many patterns for a trivial game), so it tests judgment (YAGNI) as much as modelling. Efficient win-checking is a nice discussion point.
solutions: Core entities
Game, Board (n×n grid of cells), Player, Move/Position, and a result/GameState (in-progress, win, draw).
Turn management
Alternate players; validate the target cell is empty and in-bounds before placing.
Win detection
Check the affected row, column, and (if on them) the two diagonals after each move — O(n) per move instead of scanning the whole board.
Extensibility (light)
Generalise to n×n and k-in-a-row; optionally a WinStrategy if truly needed — but don't over-pattern a simple game.
Judgment
State explicitly that you're keeping it simple (YAGNI). Interviewers reward not forcing Strategy/Factory/Observer where they add nothing.
topics.papers: Sources: github.com/ashishps1/awesome-low-level-design; algomaster.io; hellointerview.com (patterns emerge, don't force). Verified.
topics.takeaway: Keep it simple and say so. Check only the affected row/col/diagonals for O(n) win detection. Over-engineering is the real trap.
topics.deepDive:
Tic-tac-toe is deceptively about restraint. Because the domain is tiny, a candidate who has just crammed a pattern catalogue will instinctively reach for a Factory to make players, a Singleton for the board, an Observer to announce wins, and a Strategy for placement — and every one of those is a red flag here, because none earns its keep. The interviewer is often specifically checking whether you can calibrate: apply just enough structure and no more. The strong move is to build the small clean version — Game orchestrating a Board of cells, a Player, moves that validate the cell is empty and in-bounds, and a GameState result — and to say out loud, 'I'll keep this minimal; there's no real variation point that justifies more patterns yet (YAGNI).' That sentence is itself a scored signal.

The one genuinely interesting technical point is win detection. The naive approach re-scans the entire board after every move; the better approach observes that only the row, column, and — when the move lands on one — the two diagonals of the just-placed mark can possibly have completed, so you check those in O(n) rather than O(n²). An even slicker version maintains per-row, per-column, and per-diagonal counters that increment on each placement, giving O(1) win checks; mentioning this optimisation shows algorithmic awareness without over-designing the class structure. Generalising the board to n×n and to k-in-a-row is the natural extensibility question, and it's a legitimate place to introduce a small abstraction — but only because the requirement actually changed.

The rest is careful edge-case handling: reject moves to occupied or out-of-bounds cells, detect a draw when the board fills with no winner, and manage clean turn alternation. Because the problem is so contained, the differentiator is entirely judgment and communication: a candidate who builds the minimal correct design, optimises win detection thoughtfully, and explicitly resists gratuitous patterns will out-score one who produces an elaborate pattern-laden cathedral for a child's game. Tic-tac-toe rewards knowing when not to.

mcqs.q: What is the most common trap in the tic-tac-toe LLD problem?
options: Over-engineering it with unnecessary patterns (violating YAGNI)
Using too few classes to be legal
mcqs.explanation: The domain is tiny; bolting on Factory/Singleton/Observer/Strategy where they add nothing signals poor judgment. Keep it minimal and say so.

mcqs.q: What's the efficient way to check for a win after a move?
options: Rescan the entire board every move
Check only the affected row, column, and (if on them) the diagonals — O(n)
Only check at the end of the game
mcqs.explanation: Only the just-placed mark's row, column, and relevant diagonal(s) can complete, so check those in O(n) (or O(1) with running counters).

mcqs.q: When IS it legitimate to introduce a small abstraction in tic-tac-toe?
options: When a requirement actually changes — e.g. generalising to n×n and k-in-a-row
Always add at least four patterns
Only if the interviewer is from Google
mcqs.explanation: Abstraction is justified by a real change in requirements (n×n, k-in-a-row), not added speculatively — that's the YAGNI/OCP balance.

topics.name: Design Snake & Ladder
topics.premise: Model the board game: a numbered board with snakes and ladders (jumps), multiple players, dice rolls, turn management, and win detection when a player reaches the final cell. A clean, contained modelling exercise often used to test entity design and turn loops.
topics.frequency: Tier-2 classic; on the Prakalpana 7-problem set and most lists.
topics.why: Straightforward entities with a clear game loop; good for demonstrating clean modelling, a Dice abstraction (swappable for testing), and jump handling without over-engineering.
solutions: Core entities
Game, Board (cells 1..N), Jump/BoardEntity (snake or ladder with start/end), Player (with position), Dice, and a game loop.
Board & jumps
Represent snakes and ladders uniformly as 'jumps' (start → end); after moving, if the landing cell has a jump, apply it. Snake: end < start; ladder: end > start.
Dice abstraction
A Dice class (or interface) so you can inject a deterministic dice in tests; supports 1..6 or multiple dice.
Turn management
Queue of players; each turn rolls, advances, applies any jump, checks win. Handle overshoot rule (must land exactly on N, or not — clarify).
Edge cases
Overshoot behaviour, multiple players on a cell, exact-finish rule, a jump chaining into another (usually disallowed — clarify).
topics.takeaway: Model snakes and ladders uniformly as 'jumps' (start→end). Abstract the Dice so you can test deterministically. Clarify the exact-finish rule.
topics.deepDive:
Snake & Ladder is a modelling-hygiene problem: there's little algorithmic depth, so the interviewer reads how cleanly you name entities and structure the game loop. The single best modelling insight is to unify snakes and ladders. Beginners create separate Snake and Ladder classes with near-identical fields; the elegant move is one Jump (or BoardEntity) with a start and end cell — a ladder is simply a jump where end > start and a snake one where end < start. The board then holds a map from cell to jump, and the move logic is uniform: advance the token, and if the landing cell has a jump, teleport to its end. This collapses duplicated code and is a small, genuine application of finding the right abstraction.

The second worthwhile decision is abstracting the Dice. Making Dice a class (or interface) with a roll() method looks trivial, but it pays off two ways: it lets you support multiple dice or a custom face count by changing one place, and — the part that impresses — it makes the game testable, because you can inject a deterministic/mock dice that returns a scripted sequence instead of random numbers. Mentioning testability here scores on the Testing dimension and shows you think about how the code will be verified, not just how it runs.

The rest is a clean turn loop and honest edge-case clarification. Players sit in a queue; each turn rolls, advances, applies any jump, and checks whether they've reached the final cell. Several rules are genuinely ambiguous and worth surfacing rather than assuming: does a player have to land exactly on cell N or does overshooting just cap/bounce? Can a jump's destination itself trigger another jump (usually disallowed to prevent loops)? What happens with multiple players on one cell? Asking these is the clarifying-requirements signal. As with tic-tac-toe, resist over-engineering — no elaborate pattern is needed — and the differentiator becomes the uniform-jump abstraction, the testable Dice, and disciplined edge-case handling.

mcqs.q: What is the cleanest way to model snakes and ladders?
options: Two separate unrelated classes with duplicated fields
One 'Jump' with start and end — ladder if end>start, snake if end<start
Hard-code every snake and ladder as a method
mcqs.explanation: Unify them as a single Jump(start,end): a ladder has end>start, a snake end<start — collapsing duplicated code.

mcqs.q: Why abstract the Dice into its own class/interface?
options: So a deterministic mock dice can be injected for testing (and to vary face count)
To avoid randomness entirely in production
mcqs.explanation: A Dice abstraction makes the game testable (inject scripted rolls) and lets you change dice count/faces in one place.

mcqs.q: Which is a genuinely ambiguous rule worth clarifying up front?
options: Whether a player must land exactly on the final cell or overshooting is allowed
mcqs.explanation: The exact-finish/overshoot rule (and whether jumps chain) is ambiguous — asking is the clarifying-requirements signal.

tiers.name: System-flavoured LLD
tiers.blurb: Problems that look like mini-systems but are graded at the class level: thread-safety, data-structure composition, and pluggable policy. These lean hardest on concurrency and are common at Amazon/Uber.

topics.name: Design an LRU Cache
topics.premise: Design a fixed-capacity cache with O(1) get and put that evicts the least-recently-used entry when full. The canonical answer is a hash map + doubly-linked list. Frequently extended to LFU, TTL expiry, and — the LLD twist — a thread-safe version.
topics.frequency: Tier-1; appears on the Prakalpana 7-set, awesome-low-level-design, and straddles the algo/LLD boundary. Very common.
topics.why: It's the cleanest test of composing two data structures for O(1) operations, and its thread-safe variant is a favourite for probing concurrency (locking granularity, race conditions) at the class level.
solutions: Hash map + doubly-linked list
Map key→node for O(1) lookup; a doubly-linked list orders nodes by recency. On access, move the node to the front (MRU); evict from the back (LRU) when over capacity.
O(1) operations
get(): map lookup + move node to front. put(): insert/update, move to front, evict tail if over capacity. Both O(1).
Thread-safety (the LLD twist)
Guard with a lock. Discuss granularity: a single lock is simple and correct; finer-grained/striped locking or a concurrent structure improves throughput. Beware the get()-also-mutates-order race.
Extensibility
An EvictionPolicy interface (LRU, LFU, FIFO) makes the policy swappable (Strategy) — a common follow-up. TTL adds expiry timestamps.
Generics & interface
A clean Cache<K,V> interface with get/put; the LRU implementation behind it.
topics.takeaway: Hash map + doubly-linked list = O(1) get/put. The LLD twist is thread-safety — discuss lock granularity and the get()-mutates-order race. An EvictionPolicy interface makes it Strategy-extensible.
topics.deepDive:
The LRU cache sits on the boundary between the algorithms round and LLD, and which side an interviewer emphasises tells you what to stress. The data-structure core is the same either way: a hash map gives O(1) key lookup, and a doubly-linked list maintains recency order so that the most-recently-used sits at the front and the least-recently-used at the back. The map's values are the list nodes themselves, which is the trick that makes everything O(1) — given a key you jump straight to its node and can unlink/relink it in constant time without scanning. get() finds the node and moves it to the front; put() inserts or updates, moves to front, and if capacity is exceeded, drops the tail node (and its map entry). The doubly-linked part matters: you need O(1) removal of an arbitrary node, which a singly-linked list can't give you.

What turns this from an algorithm answer into an LLD answer is the thread-safety discussion, and it's where senior signal lives. The non-obvious hazard is that get() is not read-only — it mutates recency order by moving a node to the front — so two concurrent get()s, or a get racing a put, can corrupt the list or the counts if unguarded. The simplest correct fix is a single lock around both operations; you should say that plainly, then discuss the trade-off: one coarse lock serialises all access and can bottleneck a hot cache, whereas finer-grained approaches (lock striping, or a concurrent map plus careful list synchronisation) raise throughput at the cost of complexity and subtle correctness risk. Naming that trade-off, rather than silently slapping 'synchronized' on everything, is the differentiator.

The extensibility follow-up is usually 'now make it LFU' or 'add TTL'. This is the cue for an EvictionPolicy interface (Strategy): LRU, LFU, and FIFO become interchangeable implementations, and the cache depends on the abstraction (Dependency Inversion). LFU needs frequency counts (often a frequency-bucketed structure for O(1)); TTL needs per-entry expiry timestamps checked on access or swept lazily. Wrapping it all behind a clean generic Cache<K,V> interface, and enumerating edge cases (capacity zero, updating an existing key, evicting the last item), completes a design that reads as production-quality rather than a LeetCode snippet.

mcqs.q: Which data-structure combination gives O(1) get and put for an LRU cache?
options: A hash map + a doubly-linked list
mcqs.explanation: The hash map gives O(1) lookup to list nodes; the doubly-linked list maintains recency order with O(1) move/remove.

mcqs.q: What is the non-obvious concurrency hazard in an LRU cache?
options: get() mutates recency order (moves a node), so it races with other operations
mcqs.explanation: get() isn't read-only — it moves a node to the front — so concurrent gets/puts can corrupt the list unless guarded.

mcqs.q: How do you make the eviction policy (LRU/LFU/FIFO) swappable?
options: Introduce an EvictionPolicy interface (Strategy) the cache depends on
mcqs.explanation: An EvictionPolicy interface (Strategy + Dependency Inversion) lets the cache switch policies without modifying its core code.

topics.name: Design a Rate Limiter
topics.premise: Design a component that limits how many requests a client may make in a time window (e.g. 100 req/min). Compare algorithms — token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter — and make them pluggable. The LLD emphasis is thread-safety and clean strategy separation.
topics.frequency: Tier-1; on the HelloInterview list and appears frequently, often as the concurrency-focused problem.
topics.why: It's the go-to problem for testing algorithm trade-offs (accuracy vs memory vs burst handling) behind a clean Strategy interface, plus real concurrency (atomic counter updates under many threads).
solutions: Strategy — pluggable algorithms
RateLimiter interface with implementations: TokenBucket, LeakyBucket, FixedWindowCounter, SlidingWindowLog, SlidingWindowCounter. Swappable per client/route.
Token bucket
Tokens refill at a fixed rate up to a capacity; each request consumes one; allows bursts up to capacity. The most common default.
Fixed vs sliding window
Fixed window is simple but allows 2× bursts at window edges; sliding window log is accurate but memory-heavy; sliding window counter approximates it cheaply.
Thread-safety
Counter/token updates must be atomic under concurrent requests — use atomic operations or locks; the check-and-decrement must be a single critical section.
Per-client state
A map from clientId → limiter state; in distributed settings this state lives in a shared store (Redis), but the LLD focus is the in-process class design.
links: How to prepare for LLD — HelloInterview
topics.takeaway: Put each algorithm behind a RateLimiter Strategy interface. Token bucket is the sane default. The check-and-decrement must be one atomic critical section.
topics.deepDive:
The rate limiter is the interview's canonical vehicle for two things at once: comparing algorithms with real trade-offs, and getting concurrency right on a hot path. Start by putting the algorithm behind a RateLimiter interface (a single allow(clientId) → boolean method), because the whole point is that the algorithm is a swappable policy — different routes or client tiers may want different limiters, and a follow-up almost always asks you to switch or add one. That Strategy boundary is the structural signal; the algorithm choices are the depth signal.

Each algorithm trades accuracy against memory and burst behaviour, and being able to articulate that is what distinguishes a strong answer. Fixed-window counter is trivial — count requests per calendar window — but it permits a double-rate burst straddling a boundary (100 requests at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00). Sliding-window log fixes accuracy by storing a timestamp per request and counting those within the trailing window, but its memory grows with request volume. Sliding-window counter is the pragmatic middle ground, weighting the previous window's count to approximate the log cheaply. Token bucket — tokens refilling at a steady rate up to a capacity, each request spending one — is the most common default because it allows controlled bursts (up to capacity) while enforcing an average rate, and leaky bucket is its smoothing cousin that enforces a constant outflow. Naming which you'd pick and why ('token bucket, because we want to permit short bursts but cap the sustained rate') is the trade-off conversation the rubric rewards.

Concurrency is intrinsic: a rate limiter is hammered by many threads simultaneously, and the classic bug is a check-then-act race where two threads both read '99 used' and both proceed, admitting 101. The fix is to make the check-and-consume a single atomic operation — an atomic counter/compare-and-set, or a lock around the read-modify-write — and to say so explicitly. It's also worth drawing the boundary to HLD: per-client state lives in a map in-process, but at scale it moves to a shared store like Redis so limits hold across many servers; the interviewer usually wants the in-process class design here, with a nod to the distributed version. Edge cases — first request for a new client, clock skew, window boundaries — round it out. The winning shape: Strategy interface, a defensible default algorithm with stated trade-offs, and an atomic check-and-decrement.

mcqs.q: Why put the rate-limiting algorithm behind a RateLimiter interface?
options: So algorithms (token bucket, sliding window, etc.) are swappable per client/route (Strategy + OCP)
Because interfaces are mandatory in Java
mcqs.explanation: Strategy: the algorithm is a pluggable policy; different routes/tiers can use different limiters and new ones can be added without changing callers.

mcqs.q: What is the known weakness of the fixed-window counter algorithm?
options: It can allow nearly double the limit in a burst straddling the window boundary
mcqs.explanation: Requests bunched at the end of one window and start of the next can briefly reach ~2× the intended rate.

mcqs.q: What must be atomic in a concurrent rate limiter?
mcqs.explanation: A check-then-act race lets two threads both see capacity and both proceed. The check-and-consume must be a single atomic critical section.

topics.name: Design a Notification System
topics.premise: Design a service that sends notifications across multiple channels (email, SMS, push, in-app) with pluggable channels, user preferences, templating, retries, and priorities. A showcase for the Observer pattern (subscribers), Strategy/Factory (channel selection), and Decorator (layering formatting/retry).
topics.frequency: Tier-2; on the SystemDesignHandbook OOD set and appears regularly. Straddles LLD/HLD.
topics.why: It exercises Observer (notify many subscribers), Factory/Strategy (create/select the right channel), Decorator (add retry/formatting), and clean extensibility (adding a new channel must not touch existing ones — OCP).
solutions: Channel abstraction — Strategy/Factory
NotificationChannel interface (EmailChannel, SmsChannel, PushChannel, InAppChannel); a factory creates the right one. Adding a channel is a new class (OCP).
Observer
Subscribers register interest; the system notifies all relevant observers on an event (pub/sub within the service).
Decorator
Wrap a notification with formatting, retry, or throttling behaviour without subclass explosion.
User preferences & templating
Per-user channel preferences and opt-outs; templates parameterised per notification type.
Reliability
Retries with backoff, priority queue for urgent vs bulk, and idempotency to avoid duplicate sends. At scale a message queue decouples producers from senders (HLD boundary).
links: OOD interview guide — System Design Handbook
topics.takeaway: Channels behind a NotificationChannel interface (Strategy/Factory) so adding one is OCP-clean; Observer for subscribers; Decorator for retry/formatting.
topics.deepDive:
The notification system is a pattern-rich problem, but the discipline it tests is extensibility: the interviewer will say 'now add WhatsApp' and watch whether that's a one-class change or a scattered edit. So the spine of the design is a NotificationChannel interface with concrete EmailChannel, SmsChannel, PushChannel, and InAppChannel implementations, created through a factory keyed on channel type. Because the sender depends on the interface, not the concretions (Dependency Inversion), and each channel is self-contained, adding a channel is a new class plus a factory registration — textbook Open/Closed. This is the single most-graded aspect of the problem, so lead with it.

Several other patterns fit naturally, and the skill is applying them where they earn their place rather than everywhere. Observer models the pub/sub reality: an event (order shipped, price dropped) fans out to all subscribers/users interested in it, which is a clean one-to-many notify. Decorator handles cross-cutting behaviours you want to layer without a subclass explosion — wrapping a base send with retry, rate-limiting, or formatting decorators means you can compose 'email + retry + throttle' without a combinatorial class hierarchy. User preferences (which channels a user has opted into, quiet hours, opt-outs) and templating (parameterised message templates per notification type) are domain responsibilities that should live in their own components, not be smeared into the channels.

Reliability is where senior candidates add depth. Notifications must survive transient failures, so retries with exponential backoff belong in the design (often as a Decorator or a queue-consumer concern), along with a priority notion so an OTP beats a marketing blast, and idempotency keys so a retry doesn't double-send. This is also the natural place to mark the LLD/HLD boundary out loud: within one service you're designing classes, but at scale a message queue decouples the producers (things that raise events) from the senders (channel workers), giving durability and back-pressure — the interviewer usually wants the class design with a gesture at that architecture. Enumerate edge cases — user opted out of all channels, a channel provider down (fail over or queue), duplicate event — and the design reads as robust. The through-line to voice: channels are a Strategy/Factory for OCP extensibility, Observer fans events out, Decorator layers reliability, and a queue handles scale.

mcqs.q: How do you make adding a new notification channel (e.g. WhatsApp) an Open/Closed change?
options: Add an if/else branch in the sender for each channel
Implement a NotificationChannel interface as a new class + factory registration
Put all channels in one giant class
mcqs.explanation: A NotificationChannel interface with per-channel implementations (Strategy/Factory) means a new channel is a new class, not edits to existing code.

mcqs.q: Which pattern fits fanning a single event out to many interested subscribers?
mcqs.explanation: Observer models one-to-many notification: subscribers register and are notified when the event fires.

mcqs.q: Which reliability concern prevents a retry from sending a user the same alert twice?
mcqs.explanation: Idempotency keys ensure a retried send is recognised as a duplicate and not delivered twice.

topics.name: Design Splitwise
topics.premise: Design an expense-sharing app: users, groups, adding expenses split among members (equally, by exact amounts, or by percentage), tracking who owes whom, and simplifying/settling balances. The textbook Strategy-pattern problem via a SplitStrategy interface.
topics.frequency: Tier-1; on the Prakalpana 7-set and appears frequently, especially at product companies.
topics.why: The split types are a clean Strategy exercise, balance tracking tests data modelling (who-owes-whom as a graph/map), and debt simplification is a nice algorithmic extension.
solutions: Strategy — split types
SplitStrategy interface with EqualSplit, ExactSplit, PercentSplit. An expense holds a strategy; adding a new split type is a new class (OCP).
Core entities
User, Group, Expense (amount, payer, participants, split), and a Balance/BalanceSheet tracking net amounts between pairs of users.
Balance tracking
Maintain a map of (userA, userB) → net amount, updated on each expense. Represents who owes whom.
Debt simplification (extension)
Minimise the number of transactions to settle up — a classic greedy/heap algorithm on net balances. Good senior-level extension.
Validation & edge cases
Percentages sum to 100; exact amounts sum to the total; a user can't split with no participants; settling partial amounts.
topics.takeaway: SplitStrategy interface (Equal/Exact/Percent) is the core; track balances as a who-owes-whom map; debt simplification is the standout senior extension.
topics.deepDive:
Splitwise is the problem that most cleanly rewards the Strategy pattern, so the design should be organised around it. The requirement 'an expense can be split equally, by exact amounts, or by percentage — and we might add more' is the textbook trigger: define a SplitStrategy interface with a method that, given an expense total and participants, returns each participant's share, and implement EqualSplit, ExactSplit, and PercentSplit. Each Expense holds a reference to the strategy used, so computing shares is a polymorphic call and adding, say, a 'shares/weights' split later is a new class with zero edits to existing code (Open/Closed). Leading with this earns the structural signal immediately.

The data-modelling core is balance tracking, and how you represent 'who owes whom' is graded. The clean model is a map keyed by an unordered pair of users to a net amount (or a per-user map of counterparties to signed balances), updated incrementally as each expense is added: when Alice pays 900 split three ways, Bob and Carol each owe Alice 300, and those deltas fold into the running balances. Keeping this as net balances (rather than a growing log of individual debts) means a query like 'what does Bob owe Alice' is O(1) and settlement is straightforward. It's worth stating the invariant that all net balances across the system sum to zero — a good correctness check and a nice thing to verify out loud.

The senior-level extension is debt simplification: given everyone's net balance, minimise the number of transactions needed to settle up. This is a classic greedy algorithm — repeatedly match the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor (often via two heaps) — and raising it unprompted signals depth beyond the class diagram. Finally, validation is where the Testing dimension shows: percentages must sum to 100, exact amounts must sum to the total (reject otherwise), a split needs at least one participant, and partial settlements must update balances correctly. The narration that scores: split types are a Strategy for OCP, balances are a who-owes-whom map with a zero-sum invariant, and debt simplification is the greedy cherry on top.

mcqs.q: Which pattern is the core of a Splitwise design?
options: Strategy — a SplitStrategy interface for equal/exact/percent splits
mcqs.explanation: Split types (equal, exact, percentage) are interchangeable algorithms behind a SplitStrategy interface — Strategy, and OCP for new split types.

mcqs.q: How is 'who owes whom' best tracked?
options: A growing append-only log scanned on every query
A map of net balances between users, updated incrementally (sums to zero)
mcqs.explanation: Net balances per user-pair give O(1) queries and simple settlement; the system-wide invariant is that all net balances sum to zero.

mcqs.q: What is a strong senior-level extension to raise for Splitwise?
options: Adding more colours to the UI
Debt simplification — minimise the number of settle-up transactions (greedy/heaps)
mcqs.explanation: Minimising settlement transactions via a greedy match of largest creditor and debtor shows algorithmic depth beyond the class diagram.
